# Benchmarks

The comparison below is generated from a run. Everything after it was measured separately,
then written by hand, so a figure in the prose can go stale in a way a figure in the table
cannot.

## Against decimal.js and big.js

<!-- generated by bench/report.mjs -->

Measured on darwin/arm64, node 22.22.0, against decimal.js 10.6.0 and big.js 7.0.1. Every library is set to 34 digits with half-even rounding. Lower is better, and a difference inside 5% is called even because that is what the same machine returns between runs.

| operation | decem | decimal.js | big.js | vs decimal.js |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| parse a 34-digit literal | 98 ns | 222 ns | 203 ns | 2.3x faster |
| to string | 88 ns | 100 ns | 158 ns | 1.1x faster |
| add | 62 ns | 69 ns | 50 ns | 1.1x faster |
| multiply | 35 ns | 120 ns | 155 ns | 3.4x faster |
| divide, 34 digits | 237 ns | 997 ns | 4008 ns | 4.2x faster |
| compare | 64 ns | 34 ns | 14 ns | **1.9x slower** |
| sqrt, 34 digits | 1098 ns | 6419 ns | 45.6 us | 5.8x faster |
| exp, 34 digits | 5301 ns | 30.5 us | n/a | 5.8x faster |
| ln, 34 digits | 3564 ns | 42.3 us | n/a | 11.9x faster |
| add, 400 digits | 207 ns | 319 ns | n/a | 1.5x faster |
| multiply, 400 digits | 249 ns | 56.5 us | n/a | 227.2x faster |

Reproduce with `node bench/versus.mjs`, and regenerate this section with `node bench/report.mjs`. Each library is driven from its own file under `bench/peers/`, so if one of them is being called wrongly the mistake is in one file and a pull request against it is the fix. Results from other processors are worth more to us than any number here, since every figure above comes from one machine.

### Where it loses

**compare**, 1.9x slower against decimal.js. Both peers keep digits in a form that can be scanned directly, while decem has to align two exponents before it can compare. It is the cheapest operation in the table, so there is nothing else in the row to amortise that against.

### What the widest row is not

Multiplication is not the same operation on both sides. decem's is exact and keeps every digit; decimal.js rounds the product to its configured precision. At 34 digits the inputs are short enough that both results are exact anyway, so that row is a direct comparison. At 400 digits it is not: decem returns an 800-digit exact product where decimal.js returns 34 rounded digits, and decem is still 227 times faster, because a base-1e7 array multiplies in O(n squared) and a BigInt does not. The ratio is reported with that difference stated, not left for the reader to find.

`toString` is cached on a decem value, so a fresh value is built on every iteration. Timing the cache would be timing a property read.

None of this is the reason to choose decem. Every row here is tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, which is not where an application spends its time. These numbers are here so that the contract does not have to be paid for in speed.

<!-- end generated -->

## Across runtimes

The regression baseline is kept per runtime, not averaged, because the difference
is large and consistent.

| Operation | Node (V8) | Bun (JSC) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `parse/34` | 93 ns | 127 ns |
| `toString/fresh` | 89 ns | 320 ns |
| `add/34` | 60 ns | 266 ns |
| `mul/34` | 35 ns | 95 ns |
| `div/34` | 226 ns | 475 ns |
| `cmp/34` | 56 ns | 174 ns |
| `sqrt/34` | 1,039 ns | 1,053 ns |
| `exp/34` | 7,424 ns | 5,729 ns |
| `div/400` | 2,744 ns | 2,282 ns |
| `exp/400` | 176.4 us | 165.2 us |

Bun is two to four times slower on the small-value rows and comparable or better on the
large ones. Raw `BigInt` multiplication is similar between the two engines. What differs
is allocation, collection and object creation, which dominate when the values are small
because every operation here returns a new object.

## The measurement protocol

Numbers without a method are not evidence. The protocol lives in
[`../bench/protocol.mjs`](../bench/protocol.mjs), which defines it: one cold run recorded
separately, warmup discarded, empty-loop overhead subtracted, median of nine rounds, and
an interquartile-range gate that marks a measurement noisy above 15% of the median and
excludes it from regression judgement instead of letting noise read as a change.

A detected regression is measured a second time and only fails if it repeats. The IQR
catches variation within a run but not drift between runs, and sustained machine load
produces a stably slow measurement that looks exactly like a regression. Addition once
appeared 1.31x slower that way.

## Why a BigInt mantissa

The 400-digit rows above come from the representation. decimal.js stores the mantissa as
a `number[]` in base 1e7, the largest base whose products stay inside 2^53, and the right
choice in 2014, four years before `BigInt`. Multiplication, ns per operation:

| Digits | base-1e7 array | BigInt | Array slower by |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | 32 | 8 | 4.1x |
| 448 | 71 us | 246 ns | 288x |
| 3,584 | 8.1 ms | 9.5 us | 854x |
| 14,336 | 132 ms | 87 us | 1,524x |

There is no size at which the array wins, not even at one word, and the engines' `BigInt`
is sub-quadratic so the gap widens without bound.

It is the weaker choice in one place, and that place is in the table above: a `BigInt` is
binary, so every decimal digit costs a division, and `compare` has to align two exponents
where an already-decimal array can scan.
